strengths: The core idea is simple, clean, and timely: repurposing classic SSL pretext tasks (rotation, jigsaw, contrastive, patch position) as intrinsically verifiable rewards for GRPO-based post-training of VLMs addresses a genuine bottleneck (scalable rewards without human labels or LLM judges).

The empirical study is broad and systematic: vision-language benchmarks (MMBench, SEED-Bench), vision-centric classification (ImageNet-1K subsets), task-difficulty scaling, model-size scaling (3B vs 7B), task combination, and a cross-domain extension to text-attributed graphs, with detailed per-task results in the appendix.

The paper honestly reports negative and nuanced results: contrastive rewards degrade some downstream tasks, naive reward combination is non-additive, and gains shrink at 7B scale. The 'difficulty-capacity matching' (Goldilocks) analysis is a useful, actionable design principle.

Qualitative analyses (attention-map comparisons, case studies in Appendix E/F) provide mechanistic plausibility for the claim that SSL4RL improves visual grounding and reduces language bias, and reward curves (Appendix D) document that these 'trivial' tasks are genuinely hard for the base VLM.
Hyperparameters, training setup, prompt formats, and evaluation protocol are described in enough detail to support reproducibility, and the authors commit to releasing code.
weaknesses: Missing the most important baseline: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the exact same SSL tasks/data. Without this, it is impossible to disentangle whether the gains come from the RL (GRPO) formulation itself or simply from additional training on perception-heavy data. Related self-training/RL baselines (e.g., STaR-style or existing VLM post-training methods) are also absent, so the claimed advantage over alternatives is not established.

The headline gains (e.g., +39 points on MMBench Relation Reasoning) are suspiciously large and could partially reflect learned answer formatting rather than genuine reasoning improvements; no probing or format-controlled evaluation is provided to rule this out. Single-run results without variance estimates or significance tests further weaken the reliability of the reported differences.

The training corpus is never clearly specified (which images, how many, how related to the evaluation distributions), raising potential train/test leakage or distribution-alignment confounds, particularly for the ImageNet evaluation where the model is fine-tuned on in-domain images.

Generalization is limited: only Qwen2.5-VL (3B/7B) is tested, the contrastive reward is a rather loose binary-classification surrogate for InfoNCE, and the 'anti-commonsense' explanation for rotation's effectiveness is speculative rather than empirically validated.

Evaluation coverage is modest (MMBench, SEED-Bench, ImageNet subsets); no harder or held-out multimodal reasoning benchmarks (e.g., MMMU, MathVista, Video-MME) are used, so claims about 'reasoning' improvements rest on narrow evidence. There is also no explicit limitations section, though several limitations are discussed inline.

The graph extension (Section 5) is a thin demonstration: the 7B results show near-zero or negative average gains and severe regressions on some datasets (e.g., Products dropping from 50.50 to 43.47/48.89), which the text somewhat underplays.

strengths: The core idea is clean and clearly articulated: SSL pretext tasks provide intrinsically verifiable targets, which can serve as dense reward signals for GRPO-based post-training without human labels or LLM judges. This is a sensible answer to a real bottleneck (scarcity of verifiable rewards outside math/code).

The empirical study is broad: two VLM scales (3B/7B), two multimodal benchmarks (MMBench, SEED-Bench), a vision-centric ImageNet evaluation, and a graph-domain extension, with reasonably detailed appendix tables.

The ablations are the strongest part of the paper: task difficulty scaling (the 'Goldilocks' finding that increasing difficulty helps Contrastive but hurts Rotation/Jigsaw), model-size scaling (diminishing returns at 7B), and the non-additivity of combined rewards. These are useful design insights for future work.
Qualitative analyses (attention heatmaps, case studies of reduced language bias in Appendix E/F) provide some mechanistic color, and the paper is generally well written and easy to follow.
An honest limitations-adjacent discussion exists: the paper openly reports that Contrastive degrades reasoning benchmarks and that naive reward combination underperforms the best single reward.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the framework is essentially a combination of well-known components—2015-2018-era pretext tasks (rotation, jigsaw, context prediction) plus standard GRPO. Reinforced Pre-Training [28], which the paper itself cites, already uses next-token prediction as an RL reward at pretraining. The framing as a 'novel framework' overstates what is, at heart, an empirical study of applying existing RL tooling to existing SSL objectives.

A critical baseline is missing: supervised fine-tuning (or simple cross-entropy training) on the exact same SSL-formatted data. Without this, it is impossible to attribute the gains to the RL procedure rather than simply to additional multimodal training on image-heavy data. Similarly, there is no comparison against GRPO with other simple verifiable rewards or against RLHF-style baselines, so the claim that SSL rewards are uniquely valuable is unsupported.

No statistical rigor: results are single runs with no seeds, variance, or significance tests. Some reported gains are small (e.g., 1.13 points average on MMBench-7B, with one category going down), and with three to four variants per table, cherry-picking of 'maximal improvement' rows (best per column) is a questionable reporting practice that inflates apparent effect sizes.

The headline 39-point jump on Relation Reasoning and 19.6 points on Visual Reasoning are suspiciously large relative to the other categories, and no analysis is given of why these specific categories improve so dramatically. Combined with the near-chance base-model accuracy mentioned for rotation, this raises concerns about benchmark contamination or format effects that the paper does not address.

The graph extension is superficial and internally inconsistent: Table 5 lists 'Qwen2.5-VL-3B'—a vision-language model—as the base for text-attributed graph tasks, and it is unclear how images and graph structure are even represented to the model. The section reads more like a demonstration than a validated generalization, and the choice of a general-purpose LLM rather than a graph model undermines the claim of cross-domain generality.

Mechanistic claims are under-evidenced: explanations such as 'anti-commonsense learning' from rotation priors and 'sharper attention' rest on a handful of anecdotal attention maps averaged over all heads/layers, with no quantitative grounding.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the Reproducibility Statement ends mid-sentence ('we will release our code') and no code or data splits are currently available; several implementation details needed for exact replication (e.g., how Contrastive rewards are computed against InfoNCE-style similarity, negative pair construction) are underspecified.

The contribution claim of 'challenging the assumption that all self-supervision is equally useful' is a mild strawman; the finding that different pretext tasks transfer differently is already well known from the SSL literature.

strengths: Simple, well-motivated and clearly articulated idea: repurposing SSL pretext tasks as intrinsically verifiable rewards for GRPO-based post-training, sidestepping the need for human labels or LLM judges. The formalization (corruption function = environment, target = ground truth, reward = correctness match) is clean.

Comprehensive and largely well-controlled empirical study: four SSL tasks, two model scales (3B/7B), three benchmark families (MMBench, SEED-Bench, ImageNet-derived tasks), plus systematic ablations on task difficulty, model scale, and task combination.

The ablation analysis is the most valuable part: the 'Goldilocks' difficulty-capacity matching principle, diminishing returns at 7B, non-additivity of combined rewards, and the divergence between contrastive learning's role in pretraining vs. SSL4RL are genuine, transferable insights that go beyond a single positive result.

The paper is honest about negative results (contrastive task degrades some downstream tasks, 5x5 difficulty yields no gains for 7B, naive reward combination fails) rather than overselling, and the graph-domain extension supports the claimed generality of the paradigm.
Appendix is thorough (detailed per-dimension results, reward curves, prompt templates, case studies), and the ethics/reproducibility statements are present; LLM usage is disclosed appropriately.
weaknesses: Missing the most important control: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the same SSL pretext tasks. Without training the same model on identical (context, target) pairs with a standard supervised loss, the paper cannot establish that the RL formulation (GRPO) is what drives the gains rather than simply additional training on the pretext data or increased image exposure. This is the decisive gap in supporting the central claim that 'SSL as intrinsic reward' is the operative mechanism.

No comparison to other RL/self-reward baselines (e.g., RLVR with ground-truth answers on downstream data, RPT which is cited as closest related work, or other verifier-free RL methods). The improvements are reported only relative to the base model, making it hard to judge the contribution's relative significance.

Training data provenance is underspecified: which unlabeled images are used for the SSL reward training is not clearly stated. Given evaluation on MMBench/SEED-Bench/ImageNet, possible distributional overlap or contamination with benchmark imagery is a soundness concern that is not addressed.

The graph-domain extension has confounds: on transductive node classification benchmarks (Cora, PubMed, WikiCS), attribute-masking SSL training on the same graph can leak label-relevant information, and improvements there may largely reflect in-domain fine-tuning rather than the SSL4RL reward mechanism. Implementation details for the graph setting are thin, and the base model scores (e.g., Cora 21.80 for a strong VLM) suggest a fragile evaluation setup; the Link task even degrades Products (7.93 -> 4.91).

Presentation issues: 'Maximal Improvement' rows take the per-category maximum across four different trained models, which inflates apparent gains; the abstract claims '9% on MMBench and 8% on SEED-Bench' while the text reports 7.39 and 8.94 percentage points, mixing percentages and percentage points; reproducibility statement is incomplete (sentence truncated, no code/data link at submission time).

Evaluation is limited to a single model family (Qwen2.5-VL), with no seed variance or significance testing; qualitative claims (sharper attention, reduced language bias) rest on anecdotal examples and a coarse attention-map analysis that is not quantitatively validated.

The contrastive reward is loosely defined (a binary classification 'imitating the InfoNCE similarity score'), which is quite different from actual contrastive objectives; conclusions about 'contrastive learning' transferring poorly may be an artifact of this proxy formulation.

strengths: The core idea is clean and appealing: self-supervised pretext tasks provide intrinsically verifiable targets that can be repurposed as dense reward signals for GRPO-based RL on VLMs, avoiding human labels, LLM-judges, and handcrafted verifiers.

The empirical study is unusually comprehensive for this line of work: four SSL tasks evaluated across six+ VQA benchmarks, open-ended captioning (CapArena), ImageNet classification, three model scales (3B/4B/7B), two base model families (Qwen2.5-VL, Gemma3), and difficulty scaling ablations.

The comparison against the Golden-3B oracle (VLM-R1-style RL with golden downstream answers, Appendix G) is a thoughtful and honest contextualization, showing SSL rewards close much of the gap to idealized task-specific rewards without using downstream labels.

The design-principle analysis is genuinely informative: (i) task effectiveness in the RL setting diverges from pre-training intuition (position prediction is highly effective; weak contrastive augmentation causes negative transfer), (ii) a 'Goldilocks' difficulty-capacity matching principle supported by 7B vs 3B results and finer-grained corruption ablations, and (iii) non-additivity of naive reward combination. The 7B results showing diminishing returns, and the harder Mask/Hard-Negative tasks partially recovering them (Table 27-28), are useful findings.

Generalization beyond the training benchmarks is checked: gains of ~7.27% on held-out benchmarks (V*, RealWorldQA, BLINK, MME-RealWorld-Lite) that were not part of the training distribution, plus a graph-domain extension that reproduces the difficulty-capacity matching pattern.
Hyperparameters, prompts, training/eval protocols, reward curves, entropy, and response-length trajectories are provided, and code release is promised, supporting reasonable reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest. The core mechanism—rule-based RL rewards on image transformations—is essentially an extension of Jigsaw-R1 [52] (explicitly acknowledged) and overlaps with concurrent work (Spatial-SSRL [36]). The 'framework' is more of a systematic empirical study than a new method; the technical formalism (Section 3) is thin, and the contrastive reward definition is vague ('imitating the InfoNCE similarity score').

Missing a critical control: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the same SSL tasks. The paper argues RL framing is key, but never compares against directly SFT-ing the model on the identical corrupted-input/target pairs with the same data. Without this, the claimed advantage of the RL formulation over standard supervised SSL fine-tuning is unsupported.

Benchmark contamination / domain-adaptation confound: the training data (Base Set ~4,000 samples from MMBench; Full Set ~118,000 including MMBench and SEED-Bench) is drawn from the same benchmarks used for headline evaluation (Tables 1, 23). Even though SSL labels are self-supervised, training on the evaluation benchmark's images and question format likely inflates the reported gains (e.g., the +39.00 point jump on MMBench Relation Reasoning, trained on MMBench data with 90° rotation labels, is hard to interpret as general reasoning improvement). The held-out benchmark results mitigate but do not eliminate this concern.

No statistical rigor: single training runs, no seeds, no variance or significance estimates, while many conclusions hinge on gaps of 1-2 points (e.g., data-scaling gains of +1.30% and +1.04%, 7B gains of +1.36%).

The graph extension is under-analyzed and its baselines look unreliable: a text-only graph task solved by a VL model (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) scoring 21.8% on Cora and improving by +34 points suggests the model was largely learning output format/data distribution rather than graph reasoning; no comparison to standard GNN or LLM-for-graph baselines is provided.

Mechanistic claims ('anti-commonsense' learning from rotation, 'sharper attention', 'reduced language bias') rest on anecdotal qualitative examples and cherry-picked attention visualizations (Appendix L), not systematic analysis; they are plausible hypotheses rather than supported conclusions.

Some results are internally awkward and insufficiently discussed, e.g., Position has a GPT-Score of 0.00 on CapArena (Table 2/25) yet is claimed to 'consistently improve'; the Contrastive task sometimes underperforms base model substantially on SEED-Bench (Table 23) and the explanation relies on unverified hypotheses.

The paper presents engineering insights but limited theoretical grounding for when/why an SSL task transfers; the takeaways, while useful, are framed more confidently than the single-run evidence warrants.

strengths: The paper is an ambitious empirical study: it evaluates four SSL pretext tasks (rotation, jigsaw, contrastive, position) as verifiable RL rewards across vision-language reasoning, image captioning, ImageNet classification, and a graph extension, with extensive ablations on data volume, model scale, base model choice, task difficulty, and task combinations.

The analysis of when SSL tasks help or hurt is genuinely informative: the finding that contrastive objectives degrade downstream performance with weak augmentations but recover with stronger ones, the non-additivity of combined rewards, and the 'difficulty-capacity matching' observation (diminishing returns from 3B to 7B) are honest, useful negative results that go beyond a simple 'our method works' narrative.

The comparison against an oracle 'Golden-3B' baseline trained with ground-truth downstream rewards is a valuable contextualization, showing SSL-derived rewards close much of the gap without any labeled downstream data.
Training dynamics (reward, entropy, response-length curves) are reported, and qualitative analyses (attention maps, case studies) support the claimed mechanism of reduced language bias.
The framework is clearly formalized, and the writing is generally easy to follow.
weaknesses: Missing the most important control: a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baseline trained on the identical SSL data with the same labels. Without it, it is impossible to determine whether the gains come from RL optimization per se or simply from exposure to the SSL-augmented data, format practice, and answer-style alignment. This is a decisive evidential gap for the central claim that RL with SSL rewards is the effective ingredient.

Serious contamination concern in the evaluation protocol: the training corpora are drawn from the very benchmarks used for evaluation (e.g., ~4,000/18,000 MMBench samples in Table 4, MMBench+SEED-Bench mixtures, and ImageNet-derived data), and models are then evaluated on those same benchmarks. Even though SSL targets are self-generated, the model sees the benchmark images and question distribution during training, which confounds the reported downstream improvements. A strictly held-out evaluation is needed.

No statistical rigor: results appear to be single runs without error bars, seeds, or significance testing, while many reported ablation deltas (e.g., +1.04% to +1.36% average gains at 7B, 0.86% on SEED-Bench) are within a plausible noise range.

Evidence of carelessness: in Appendix Table 8 (7B MMBench), the Contrastive and Position rows are numerically identical, strongly suggesting a copy-paste/data-reporting error; the abstract contains an unfinished sentence ('open-sourced at          with models hosted...'), and there are typos such as 'SSR4RL'. These undermine confidence in the reported numbers.

Novelty is modest: the core idea—reformulating a self-supervised pretext task as a verifiable RL reward—is a fairly direct composition of known components, and the paper itself acknowledges Jigsaw-R1 [52] as the direct precursor; the concurrent Spatial-SSRL [36] further narrows the contribution. What remains is a systematization/generalization, which is useful but not a fundamental advance.

The graph extension is unconvincing: the base Qwen2.5-VL-3B scores near chance on Cora (21.80%), so the +34-point jump likely reflects escaping a degenerate baseline and learning answer formats rather than meaningful structural reasoning; there is no comparison to standard GNN or graph-LLM baselines, making the claimed 'significant gains' difficult to interpret.

Internal inconsistency in methodology framing: the paper motivates SSL4RL by criticizing LLM-as-a-judge rewards as 'biased, noisy,' yet its open-ended captioning evaluation (CapArena) relies entirely on a GPT-4o judge, and the Contrastive task's binary reward is described as 'imitating' InfoNCE rather than being a genuinely verifiable target. The Figure 7/Contrastive example also shows visually distinct images labeled 'positive,' raising questions about task data quality.
Some mechanistic claims ('anti-commonsense' learning, the two-stage entropy interpretation) are speculative and supported only by narrative, not targeted experiments.
Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: code is only promised ('we will release our code'), with no anonymized repository provided for verification.

strengths: The core idea—repurposing SSL pretext tasks (rotation, jigsaw, contrastive, position) as intrinsically verifiable RL rewards for VLM post-training—is simple, well-motivated, and addresses a real bottleneck (scalable reward signals where external verifiers are absent).

The empirical study is unusually comprehensive: multiple models (Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B, Gemma3-4B), many benchmarks (MMBench, SEED-Bench, V*, RealWorldQA, BLINK, MME-RealWorld-Lite, CapArena, ImageNet-1K), plus a graph-domain extension demonstrating generality.

The paper reports negative and nuanced results honestly: contrastive SSL degrades downstream performance at default difficulty, naive reward combination does not help, and gains diminish from 3B to 7B. The 'Goldilocks difficulty' and 'difficulty-capacity matching' takeaways are genuinely useful design principles.

The oracle comparison (Golden-3B trained with ground-truth answer rewards, Appendix G) is a valuable contextualization, showing SSL4RL closes most of the gap to an idealized task-specific reward without using any downstream labels.

Supporting analyses (reward/entropy/response-length curves, robustness under perturbations, attention-map visualizations, prompt templates) add transparency, and the paper includes reproducibility and ethics statements.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: Jigsaw-R1 (Wang et al., 2025) already established rule-based visual RL with jigsaw puzzles for MLLMs, and concurrent work (Spatial-SSRL, Liu et al. 2025) covers similar self-supervised RL ideas. The main contribution is a systematic extension to multiple tasks/domains rather than a fundamentally new method.

Potential train/test image leakage undermines headline numbers: the Base training set (~4k samples) is drawn from MMBench and the Extended Set from MMBench+SEED-Bench, yet evaluation is on MMBench and SEED-Bench. Even if questions differ, the model may see evaluation images during SSL training, inflating the largest claimed gains (+9% MMBench, +8.94% SEED). Gains on benchmarks not used for training are notably smaller (e.g., +7.27% avg on V*/RealWorldQA/BLINK/MME-RealWorld-Lite), suggesting part of the improvement may be exposure to in-distribution images.

A critical baseline is missing: supervised fine-tuning (cross-entropy) on the same corrupted SSL data, or continued SSL pre-training on the same images/compute. Without this, the claim that the RL formulation (rather than simply additional visual training data) drives the improvements is not established.
Results are single-run with no error bars, seeds, or significance testing, which is problematic for small margins (e.g., 7B gains of +1.36 on MMBench, and some 7B tasks slightly below base).

The graph extension is under-controlled: the Qwen2.5-VL base model scores 30.09% on Cora-class tasks (e.g., 21.8% on Cora), so large gains (up to +34) mainly reflect a very weak starting point; there is no comparison against actual GNN or graph-SSL baselines, limiting the significance of the 'generality' claim.

The contrastive reward is described vaguely ('binary classification imitating the InfoNCE similarity score'), and the task collapses to near-trivial difficulty (reward reaches 1.0 within 50 epochs), making the task-comparison analysis partly an artifact of how difficulty was configured.

Some presentation inconsistencies and oddities: CapArena GPT-Score of 0.00 for both the base and Position models complicates interpretation of the captioning claim; Choice-20 appears as Choice10 in Appendix Table 13; minor typos persist (e.g., 'Vision Questioning Answer', 'SSR4RL', 'Trails on Harder SSL4RL tasks').
